articles.title: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare Story Recap – What You Need To Know Ahead of MW4
articles.summary: The whole story of Call of Duty's rebooted Modern Warfare saga ends in this month's MW4. Catch up on everything you need to know before you play, including all the stuff that happened in Warzone's cutscenes.
articles.body:
It’s fair to say that, across the three games in the reboot series so far, Call of Duty: Modern Warfare’s story has been far from a simple one. With the amount of action happening during each mission, combined with key plot points occurring outside of the core campaigns in places like Warzone’s Verdansk, it can be difficult to keep track.

Thankfully, we’re here to give you as succinct a summary as we can of the story so far ahead of Modern Warfare 4 ’s release. With Infinity Ward’s saga set to come to an end imminently, let’s recap how we got here. Warning: may contain a lot of chasing stolen missiles around the world.

2019’s Modern Warfare reboot tells the story of Task Force 141’s creation. That’s the elite team of operatives helmed by Call of Duty veteran Captain John Price (but not the same John Price who was in the original Modern Warfare, nor the John Price who was in the original two Call of Dutys. Look, we did say this was complicated).

But we’re already getting ahead of ourselves. At the beginning of Modern Warfare’s campaign, before 141 is established, Price and the British SAS are working with CIA Chief Kate Laswell to help recover highly valuable gas used in the creation of chemical weapons. The opening mission, in which you play as CIA agent Alex Keller, details the theft of the gas, as an unidentified team steals it en route to the fictional country of Urzikstan. The heist intensifies tension between Russia and the West.

The next day, that tension is further ratcheted. An Urzik-connected terrorist group called Al-Qatala attacks London’s Piccadilly Circus, bringing Kyle “Gaz’ Garrick into the picture. In order to hunt down the atrocity’s perpetrators, he teams up with Price to raid a London home and locate the whereabouts of Al-Qatala’s leader, Omar “The Wolf” Sulaman. It turns out that he can be found in Urzikstan’s Ramaza Hospital.

Alex, conveniently, is already in Urzikstan, after agreeing to team up with the state’s Liberation Force leader, Farah Karim. She wants to get rid of a Russian general, Roman Barkov, who has occupied her home country. Alex makes it his mission to help, and in turn, Farah will aid in recovering the stolen gas — something she doesn’t realise will be found far closer to home than she could imagine.

Alex and a crack Marine unit successfully capture “The Wolf” from his hospital hideout and hold him at the US embassy. Sulaman’s lieutenant, Jamal “The Butcher” Rahar, isn’t very happy about this, though, so he attacks the embassy in an effort to extract his boss. Despite the best efforts of Alex, Farah, and the newly arrived Price and Gaz, Rahar succeeds.

The team is back to square one. Farah has a plan, though – ambush Al-Qatala as they drive along the “Highway of Death” and take back their former captive. After a bit of long-range sniping, this risky mission goes totally awry. The Russian forces turn up, attacking both the terrorists and Farah’s Urzikstan Liberation Force. As if things couldn’t get any worse for her, Farah then finds out that it was her own brother and fellow freedom fighter, Hadir, who stole the chemicals during the campaign’s first mission. He deploys them in a massive explosion, killing both the Al-Qatala and Russian forces, and leaving Alex and Farah barely alive amongst the rubble and smoke.

But what would drive Hadir, who has so far been depicted only as Farah’s loyal ally, to do war crimes? Revenge, of course. 20 years prior, a Russian invasion left both Hadir and his sister without parents. In an act of desperation born out of hatred, Hadir now joins Al-Qatala and distances himself from Farah. This event brings the interests of all the protagonists' respective factions into alignment, and so they execute a joint operation to infiltrate the terrorists’ base and find Hadir. Unfortunately, he and the stolen gas are nowhere to be found. Thankfully, the mission isn’t a total bust: the team locates and kills Sulaman, leaving the terrorist group without its leader.

The fallout is felt back in the US, though. With the chemicals' whereabouts still unknown, to make things even more difficult than they already were, the Urzikstan Liberation Force is declared a terrorist threat by the CIA. Alex isn’t best pleased, to say the least, and opts to leave his nation behind and defect to Farah’s group.

Meanwhile, it’s all kicking off in Saint Petersburg. Following a terrorist attack in the Russian city, Gaz and Price are hot on the trail of Hadir, but, again, they don’t find him. Who they do capture instead is Sulaman’s former right-hand man, Rahar, who, after a questionable spot of torture, reveals that Hadir’s next target is Barkov. And so, Price and Gaz head to the Russian general’s home, save him, and apprehend Hadir in the process. Job done? Not quite.

Hadir reveals where Barkov’s chemical weapons operation can be found, but before Price has time to head there, the CIA arrives. Laswell takes Hadir into her custody, but gives the mission her blessing. And so the quartet of Price, Gaz, Farah, and Alex reunite with Barkov’s gas factory (not a euphemism for his butt) in their sights. During the fight, Alex seemingly sacrifices himself to trigger the explosives that will bring the factory to the ground, thus ending the Russian’s operation. However, a seasonal multiplayer update later completely retcons Alex’s heroic death by revealing he actually just lost a leg – more on this weird approach to storytelling later.

It’s Barkov’s turn to be not best pleased, but before he can complete a helicopter escape, Farah kills him. This “successful” mission leads to Laswell creating Task Force 141, with their first mission set to be hunting Victor Zakhaev, a Russian ultranationalist and a familiar name to anyone who played through the original Modern Warfare.

That may be the end of the reboot’s campaign, but more story was hidden beyond its credits. Sulaman may be dead, but Al-Qatala lived on in Special Ops mode. There wasn’t a whole lot to it, apart from taking out the remaining senior figures of the organisation one by one, but it did lead to the revelation that Zakaev had been profiting from trading arms to the group.

You’d think the intention of all that would be to set up the story that the sequel would go on to tell. But no. Zakaev was dealt with, quite bizarrely, in Call of Duty’s battle royale, Warzone. In a high-stakes game of cat and mouse taking place across the city of Verdansk, it’s eventually revealed that the arms dealer has delivered weapons to numerous bunkers throughout the map.

Alex re-enters the action, because he didn’t really die and just lost a limb in that massive, gas factory-obliterating explosion, and he’s joined by new recruit, Simon “Ghost” Riley. Upon discovering Zakhaev has been using tunnels under the city to stay hidden, Price calls in yet more help, who arrive in the form of more Warzone skins to fill battle passes with. Farah and Price’s Russian confidant, Nikolai, joins the fight, reclaims the tunnels, and learns of Zakhaev’s base inside a nuclear silo. Zakhaev goes full Bond villain and threatens to launch a nuclear weapon, only for Price to shoot him and chuck him into the void. So much for that sequel, then.

Another new member of Task Force 141, John “Soap” MacTavish, then calls Price, completing the reboot’s reassembling of the original trilogy’s core cast.

Modern Warfare 2 kicks off in the Al Mazrah desert. Here, Task Force 141, on the orders of US General Shepherd, kills an Iranian General called Ghorbrani. A few months later, his second-in-command, Hassan Zyani, takes aim at the United States as a means of payback. Shepherd and Laswell catch wind of his plans, so Soap and Ghost are sent to capture Zyani before his plan comes to fruition.

The duo fail, but make a shocking discovery: an American ballistic missile is found at Zyani’s base. And so the unraveling of the mystery as to how US ordnance ended up in his possession begins — unless you played the original Modern Warfare 2, that is, and know that someone called General Shepherd isn’t to be trusted.

Not that 141 knows this yet. Their chase eventually leads to the Mexican Las Almas Cartel, who have been providing protection to Zyani. After teaming up with Mexican Special Forces’ operative Alejandro Vargas, Price and co. capture Zyani with help from Shadow Company, a mercenary group owned by Phillip Graves and commanded by Shepherd.

As is always the way when it comes to geopolitics, though, Zyani’s capture is not that simple. The team is left with no choice but to release their captive to prevent a war from erupting between the USA and Iran — a situation that the United States would never, ever allow to happen, of course.

The search for the origin of the mysterious American missile continues, the plot thickening thanks to the discovery of Russian GPS trackers in Las Almas-owned missiles. So many missiles!

Al-Qatala, the Urzi terrorist group from the first game, rears its head again, kidnapping Laswell. While Price and Gaz are once again helped by Farah to rescue her, Soap and Vargas stay in Mexico and take a captive of their own: “El Sin Nombre”, the leader of Las Almas. It turns out she’s Valeria Garza, a former accomplice of Vargas, who reveals that the missiles 141 are chasing can be found on a Gulf of Mexico oil rig.

A huge raid effort is launched, consisting of 141, Alejandro, and the very obviously shady Shadow Company (c’mon, it’s in the name) who, of course, betrays our heroes. Graves decides that everyone associated with Vargas must die, so he orders his guns for hire to commit mass murder on the streets of Mexico. 141 comes to the rescue, though, and Alejandro lives to fight another day.

It’s revealed that it was the US all along that gave missiles to its Middle Eastern allies, and it was Graves and Shepherd who spearheaded that operation. That plan hit a hitch in the road, though, when a Russian military group ambushed the convoy and stole three missiles for themselves. Shepherd covered up the whole mess to save face.

Price isn’t pleased, but focuses on the task at hand, pledging to bring Shepherd to rights once the Graves situation has been resolved. To do that, 141 storms the Shadow Company base, kills Graves, and finds out that Zyani is now in Chicago. The team beeline it to Illinois and end both Zyani’s life and plan, preventing a missile from reaching the Pentagon.

But what about the Russians who stole the missiles in the first place? Well, to quote former England football captain Wayne Rooney, “A new devil is arriving”. That would be Vladimir Makarov, the villain of the original Modern Warfare trilogy. Will he do “No Russian” all over again? Find out after we recap a bunch of storylines that happen in Modern Warfare 2’s Special Ops mode and Warzone.

Alex Keller returns in Spec Ops and asks for assistance, which is a pretty bold move considering he was AWOL for the whole of the main campaign. He’s still working on bringing down Al-Qatala for good, especially now Farah’s brother, Hadir, has become its leader. Price, Farah, and Alex eventually find Hadir, who urges them to use a nuclear missile to protect Urzikstan from the Russians. Of course, the team opts to destroy the missile and kill Hadir.

Over in Warzone, Graves’ Shadow Company lives on without its founder and is now in control of Al Mazrah. The Las Almas cartel also decides it wants a piece of the action, and so hostilities are reignited.

Elsewhere, the Dutch city of Vondel is taken over by the Peacekeepers, a new military organisation. It’s not long until it’s revealed that they are a front for the Konni Group, the Russian military unit behind the theft of Shepherd’s missiles.

A few months later, Graves arrives back on the scene – it turns out that he faked his own death, making this reboot series two for two on games featuring characters who die and then come back in seasonal updates. Appearing to have changed his tune, Graves now wants to team up with Farah’s Liberation Force and fight against the Konni Group as they move in on Al Mazrah. Things don’t go well for Shadow Company, though, who have traitors in their midst. Konni Group tears them apart from the inside and steals gas needed to create more devastating weapons, thus leading us all the way back to that little devil, Makarov.

The hell Makarov resides in would be the Modern Warfare 3 campaign itself: a selection of rehashed multiplayer maps and slices of Warzone’s Verdansk that barely manage to hold together a story. Yet, here we are.

It all kicks off with Makarov being rescued from Warzone’s gulag map. He’s been serving a life sentence in the famous PvP arena after being captured by Soap and Price prior to the events of all three games.

Meanwhile, back in Urzikstan, Makarov’s Konni Group intercepts Grave’s Shadow Company and steals missiles meant for Farah’s liberation efforts.

With Makarov now loose, Price attempts to intercept him at an abandoned facility that’s home to what remains of Barkov’s chemical materials. The mission is a disaster – Price barely escapes with his life, and Konni gets its weapon fuel.

In a dollar store rendition of the original Modern Warfare 2’s landmark “No Russian” mission, Makarov stages a terrorist attack aboard a commercial airplane, designed to make it look like Farah’s Urzikstan Liberation Force were the perpetrators. Alex helps Farah thwart this plan, though, preventing any “evidence” of ULF involvement from being discovered in the plane’s wreckage.

Price tracks a shipment heading Konni’s way, but it turns out that there are no materials inside. Instead, he discovers – drumroll, please – General Shepherd! He’s back and looking worse than ever, having been kidnapped by Makarov. Price resists the urge to kill him, and instead learns about Makarov’s plans to destroy the Gora Dam. Back to Verdansk we go.

The city’s population is saved from catastrophic flooding, and 141 shoot down a helicopter they presume is transporting Makarov. Place your bets now as to whether he’s dead or not…

Price isn’t falling for it, so he continues the search back in London, where he finds out that Makarov’s next move is to blow up the Channel Tunnel, the underwater rail line that links the UK and France. 141 quickly heads into the tunnels, but their flood-obsessed nemesis ambushes them. Soap meets a bullet to the head in as clean a kill as his name deserved.

Makarov scampers off into the darkness as Price is left to defuse a bomb. He succeeds, but it can hardly be called a victory. Later, Soap’s ashes are released from the top of a Scottish cliff, marking the end of this awkward chapter. Well, almost the end. That poignant moment is capped off with a post-credits scene showing Price finally getting his payback for all of the trouble caused by Shepherd in Mexico. He sends a silenced gunshot into the disgraced general’s skull. One villain down, at least one more to go: Makarov is still out there, waiting to meet a similar fate.

And that’s where Price and Task Force 141 are ahead of Modern Warfare 4. There are some other loose threads, but I am not going to spend time digging into whatever it was Zakhaev was doing in the Zombies mode. As a wise lady once said, “Ain’t nobody got time for that.”

So, how do you think the new string of Modern Warfare stories is going to end? We know Makarov’s clock is ticking, but will Price sacrifice himself for king and country? And what role does Mads Mikkelsen’s “The Archer” play in this whole picture? We’ll find out very soon.

Simon Cardy is a Senior Editor at IGN who can mainly be found skulking around open world games, indulging in Korean cinema, or despairing at the state of Tottenham Hotspur and the New York Jets. Follow him on Bluesky at @cardy.bsky.social .

articles.title: Valkyries defense shifted into high gear to sweep the Aces, advance to WNBA Finals
articles.summary: LAS VEGAS — The scariest sights in basketball include Chelsea Gray with the ball in a last-shot scenario. She took the dribble-handoff from A’ja Wilson, angl...
articles.body:
LAS VEGAS — The scariest sights in basketball include Chelsea Gray with the ball in a last-shot scenario. She took the dribble-handoff from A'ja Wilson, angled toward the right elbow of the free-throw line, leaned into Golden State Valkyries defender Kaila Charles, and faded back for her patented shot. Shots like this will put Gray in the Hall of Fame. Off balance. On the money.

"I thought it was in," Valkyries guard Veronica Burton said. "I was under the basket, so I got a good look."

It rattled out. A loud exhale swooshed through Michelob Ultra Arena. Angst from the Las Vegas Aces, relief from the splashes of violet in the crowd.

Gray, she of game-winner lore, grimaced as she walked to the bench to prepare for overtime.

"Shoulda hit it," Gray said. "I've hit that shot a thousand times."

But the game was over. Five minutes remained, yet these WNBA semifinals were effectively decided.

The Valkyries knew it as they sensed a team's resolve buckling beneath their pressure. Golden State locked in for the second half and rattled Las Vegas. The Valkyries' confidence graduated to conviction.

These were the defending champion Aces, to be sure. So the occasion required appropriate fear. But the heavy legs and fading force of Las Vegas, a product of injuries and the accumulated toll of years at the top of the league, revealed the gauntlet of Golden State.

This was that moment in a series, despite narratives and expectations, despite matchups and accolades, when a team realizes it's just better. Perhaps, after the talent is felt and the strategies all play out, the other team knows it, too.

That's what the Valkyries exuded in overtime of Game 3. Their defense shifted into another gear. The engine of this season, of their culture, revved like a Hellcat during the break before overtime, then proceeded to blow the doors off Las Vegas, putting the finishing touches on an 87-77 win to sweep the Aces and pause, if not end, a dynasty.

A team isn't ready to win a title until it earns the kind of conviction Golden State displayed. On the road, against the five-time MVP, with a trip to the WNBA Finals on the line, the Valkyries revealed they have a defense and a will that can make history.

"Now is our time," Burton said through the congestion that revealed her illness, echoing the message she gave in the huddle. "This is it. Like, lay it all out there. But we knew we had an extra gear. I think that's the beauty about our team, that we play so many people. We have the extra gear. We knew it was ours."

Gray's missed game-winner became a reprieve for the Valkyries, as if the game wanted to reward their tenacity.

It began at halftime, when coach Natalie Nakase showed some film that illustrated how the Valkyries had gifted the Aces an offensive groove. So in the third quarter, Golden State put the clamps down.

The Valkyries held Las Vegas to seven points in the third quarter on 2-of-16 shooting. A 17-0 Golden State run flipped the game and forced the Aces to dig deep again.

Golden State played like a team with no doubt about its defensive prowess. The pick-and-roll Las Vegas smoothly executed in the first half suddenly looked more like dental work for the Aces offense. The Valkyries fought over every screen, switched with aggression when they had to, collapsed on the ball in the paint and crashed the boards without regard for their bodies.

"They're bought in. They're on board," Wilson said. "That's what it takes to win a championship. … They're really a bought-in group from top to bottom, and it's special."

With the Aces leading 69-67 with just over two minutes remaining, Wilson got the ball on the low block with Williams on her back. The 6-foot-4 Wilson against a smaller defender had been a fruitful set for Las Vegas.

"I obviously wasn't blocking her," Williams said after the game.

Knowing that, Williams used her quickness and 6-3 wingspan to lunge around Wilson and steal the ball. Williams led the ensuing fast break, dumping it off to Kayla Thornton to tie the game. The next time down, Tiffany Hayes maneuvered the screen instead of switching, forcing Wilson into isolation against Kiah Stokes.

Stokes, the anchor of the Valkyries' defense and a three-time champion with the Aces, forced her former teammate Wilson into a contested turnaround jumper in the lane. After it missed, Burton put the Valkyries up 71-69 with a runner off the glass over Jackie Young.

The Aces had two chances to tie. But Stokes deflected and stole a pass from Young, and then blocked a Wilson turnaround. Stokes' pedigree is central to Golden State's defensive DNA.

"I could get emotional talking about it, honestly," Williams said of Stokes' impact. "She's just someone that is so appreciated by us. She just knows how to win. There's a reason she's a three-time champion."

It became increasingly clear the Valkyries' defense found its glow. Burton's go-ahead basket looked as if it might hold up. But a blown coverage, courtesy of a classically brilliant Becky Hammon after-timeout play, left Young all alone under the basket for the game-tying layup. It was the kind of mistake that dooms young teams and breathes life into older ones.

And after Williams' runner didn't drop, Gray had a chance to give the Aces life in this series. So when it missed, the inevitability kicked in.

Who they are, and who they've been, crystallized in the final five minutes of Game 3. This moment required the very elements on which they thrive. It demanded the mentality Golden State has been honing.

The fresh legs. The relentless pressure. The trust that allows one player the freedom to struggle because another will flourish. A roster not built around one transcendent scorer, but around the collective capacity to make life miserable for such scorers.

"We empty the tank," Nakase said. "We play as hard as we can for 48 minutes. With that type of style, that's probably why we had so many injuries last season. … It wasn't sustainable."

The Valkyries weren't expected to be on this precipice. Many believed they didn't belong here yet, not so soon after their inauguration. But such doubt only provided more impetus for seizing this window. They've spent all season, indeed, their entire two-year existence, crafting a defense that takes exactly what they shouldn't have.

"We've all, in one way or fashion, been the underdogs," Charles said. "Some of us have been cut from certain teams multiple times, and some of us haven't been able to get the opportunity that we deserve. So I think it's just that mentality of having the chip on our shoulder and understanding that this could be taken away unless you give 110 percent."

They're in the WNBA Finals for the first time in their history. No one's taking that away.
